scenario: AiTA for not trusting a delivery driver? | Today I ordered food off of an app- it's a third party delivery service that picks up the food and delivers your order. Once you pay online, you're given a code that you give to the delivery driver once he gives you your food (I assume that's how the drivers get paid). The app generates a time that you can expect to get your food by, and the drivers are expected to complete the delivery by then, so if you don't get your order by the promised time you often get a percentage of your order cost refunded. Drivers are not limited in how many orders they can pick up simultaneously (they use their discretion to pick up the tickets they want), but if they take too many at once, they will exceed the time limit and most likely suffer a penalty. ​ I had ordered one tea and 2 pastries, for which I only received one. I called the shop and the manager was very apologetic, offering to using the service to send me out the missing pastry ASAP. I had assumed they would just refund me through the app, but that solution was fine too. The shop paid the delivery fee, and I was given the code to give to the driver when my order arrived. About twenty minutes later, the driver called me to ask for the code, stating he was on his way. I thanked him for letting me know he was coming and hung up, to which he called back two minutes later asking for the code again. I replied that I would have it for him the minute he arrived. After another two minutes, he called back again telling me he was nearby and he was running out of time, could he have the code? I told him he would get the code when I got my food. This time I was a bit annoyed, as he knows the rules as a driver and the only way I can guarantee that my food will be delivered is to hold onto the code until my food is here. The guy snapped at me: do you not understand the code is about to expire?! And I retorted back: Well, you better hurry then, right? as nicely as possible before hanging up. I didn't want to argue any longer, but I wasn't about to risk not getting my item by giving up the code. My friend told me that I was being selfish and unkind since the guy might not get paid for the delivery. I argued that since he voluntarily picked up the ticket, he shouldn't have taken ones he couldn't deliver on time. He said something to the effect of, "thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you". ​ So, AItA? Should I have just given him the code and trusted he would still bring me my food? ​ The end of the story is, after I refused to tell him the code, I never heard from him again nor did I see my pastry. The shop manager saw the order wasn't marked as delivered and called to ask what happened, to which I told her the details. She tried to call the delivery guy then, but he had turned off his phone, so she apologized profusely, refunded me through the app, and reported him to the delivery service management. The manager said that he will either be severely disciplined or fired over this.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I need to figure out if the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details.

The person ordered food through an app, which uses third-party delivery drivers. They paid online and were given a code to give the driver upon delivery. The app estimates a delivery time, and if the driver doesn't deliver on time, they might get penalized. The drivers can pick up multiple orders, but if they take too many, they might exceed the time limit.

In this case, the person ordered one tea and two pastries but only received one. The shop manager apologized and offered to send the missing pastry. The shop paid the delivery fee, and the person was given a code for the driver. About twenty minutes later, the driver called, asking for the code, saying he was on his way. The person told him they'd give the code when the food arrives. The driver called back a couple more times, each time getting more urgent, saying he was running out of time. The person refused to give the code until the food was there. The driver snapped at them, and they retorted, telling him to hurry. They didn't want to argue and hung up. The friend told them they were being selfish and unkind because the driver might not get paid. The person argued that the driver shouldn't have taken the order if they couldn't deliver on time. The friend said the world shouldn't be full of unkind people like them. In the end, the driver didn't deliver, the shop refunded, and the driver was reported and possibly disciplined or fired.

So, the question is: Should the person have given the driver the code to trust that the driver would deliver the food? Is the person's action morally acceptable?

Let me break this down. The person was following the rules set by the app. They only give the code upon receiving the food, which is how the driver gets paid. The driver, on the other hand, was trying to get the code early, which might have been to ensure they get paid before the time limit. But the person was right in holding onto the code until the food arrives because that's how the system works.

The driver took the order, knowing the rules. If they can't deliver on time, they might face penalties. So, the person wasn't being unkind; they were just following the process. The driver's frustration is understandable, but the person's action was within their rights.

The friend's argument that the person was being unkind might not consider the system's structure. The person wasn't refusing to help; they were ensuring they received their order as per the agreement. The driver's responsibility is to manage their time and the number of orders they take. If they take too many, they might not deliver on time, which is their fault, not the customer's.

In the end, the driver didn't deliver, and the shop handled the refund and reported the driver. So, the person's action was correct in this context. They weren't being unkind; they were protecting their own interests as per the app's rules.

Therefore, the action is morally acceptable.
